text: A part goes to someone else, and rather than stay in Seoul to absorb it, the stage actor buys a ticket out of the city. What follows has no purpose beyond the excuse that starts it: a friend to visit, days to fill, and then two women, one after the other, arranged so that the second cannot help being measured against the first. Hong Sang-soo takes nearly two hours over this and declines to compress the talk. Small courtesies, restated intentions, a story told for the second time. Away from the stage the actor has no craft to fall back on, only manners, and manners run down in company. The rejection that started the trip is not much discussed. It travels anyway, unmentioned, setting the terms of every introduction he makes.

Psychic powers land on a group of high school boys, and the first use they find for them points straight at their classmates. Sion Sono spends a hundred and fifteen minutes there, a runtime that would hold a war picture and here holds one joke about adolescence: a capacity nobody asked for and nobody can switch off. The construction puts shame and ability in the same box. Yoshirō is shy to begin with, and whatever the gift does, it does it to someone whose whole project was going unnoticed. Science fiction supplies the mechanism in a line and then gets out of the way. After that it is farce, with sex kept at the level of anticipation and embarrassment, which is where the film's virgins are stuck. The comedy does not modulate. It accumulates.

A national transit strike is not the backdrop here; it is the clock. Julie has an interview for the job that would let her raise her children on better terms, and between her door and that room stand trains that are not running, platforms that are full, and the work she still has to show up for in the meantime. Eighty-eight minutes, and the shape of it is a timetable: the last connection, the children to be handed to someone, the hour by which she has to be somewhere or lose it. Eric Gravel treats logistics as pressure, which is harder than it sounds, since logistics is what films usually cut away from. No catastrophe is required. A missed departure will do. And the whole time, a woman this close to the edge of her own arrangements has to stay pleasant: on the phone, at the interview, at home.

The third wish is still owed, and the woman who granted the first two has left Le Havre without saying where. She walked into a hotel, told the man on the night desk that she was a fairy, made good on two of his wishes and went. Four genres are listed and the film appears to want all of them at once. What holds it together is bodies: ninety-three minutes in which the fantastic is less a matter of effects than of what a person can be made to do with furniture, doorways, water. Le Havre supplies concrete and cold sea, a working port rather than a place where wishes are expected. The comedy runs on that mismatch and never stops to explain it. A magical debt, pursued with the doggedness of a man chasing an unpaid invoice.

Costume adventure is a genre of contracts: dowries, titles, debts, and the question of who is permitted to refuse. A girl is placed inside that arrangement and finds in Joffrey Peyrac an attachment strong enough to make her fight it rather than merely endure it. Ariel Zeitoun stages this as adventure and not as chamber drama, a hundred and twelve minutes with a whole century of power struggle pressing on the edges, so that a private loyalty keeps running into courts, creditors and men who profit from her agreement. The pleasures are old ones and unapologetic: period surfaces, declarations made in rooms too large for them. What actually holds the film is narrower than the word destiny promises. It is a young woman working out, item by item, what her consent is worth to the people asking for it.

A scarab pushes its ball of dung uphill and the lens is close enough that the ball has texture, grain, weather. Eighty minutes in a meadow and a pond, shot from a distance nobody occupies without special equipment: magnification that makes architecture of a grass stem, slow motion for a wingbeat, time-lapse for a mosquito leaving its case. The organising idea is labour rather than taxonomy. Bees at nectar, a ladybird working through mites, a spider parcelling its catch, another spider hauling a bubble of air down to live inside it. Claude Nuridsany keeps the scale unfixed, so that two snails mating fill the frame with the gravity usually reserved for armies. Afterwards an ordinary lawn is a nuisance: too much is going on in it, at a pace that has nothing to do with anyone watching.

Both of them are fifteen, and in a South Korean middle school that single fact governs what can be said out loud. Jenny is pregnant. The film settles what the two of them intend early, without a long agony over it, and gives the remaining hour and a half to what follows: families who have to be told, a school year that continues regardless, money that neither of them earns. It is filed as a comedy, which is the choice worth noticing. Kim Ho-joon is after the strange formality of children handling adult business, the way a boy of fifteen will square his shoulders and find a serious voice. A hundred and eight minutes is a long stretch to hold that tone against a subject forever threatening to turn into a lecture. The method is to keep Jenny and Juno talking to each other, and not to the audience.

A writer who spent his fame avoiding being looked at is an awkward thing to put on a screen for a hundred and six minutes. Danny Strong takes it on anyway: the making of one novel, the noise that followed, and a man arranging his life so the noise cannot reach him. Films about authors tend to fail at the same place, since the work happens in silence and silence does not photograph. So the energy goes where drama is available, into rooms and courtship and the years before the book existed and before anyone had an opinion about it. What can be shown is the appetite for recognition that comes before the recoil from it, and how close together those two live in one person. The retreat is the famous part. The wanting is the part that can be played.
